utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis along with Belinda Pidwell and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. It's been so long since we've been in this courtroom that I have to get used to how close we all are again. Yes, if there are no preliminary matters, would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand. Mr. Zecevic, while the witness is on his way in, do you anticipate using all of your remaining anticipated 6 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I believe I informed the Trial Chamber that I will be shorter at the very beginning of my direct examination. I believe I do have another hour or so this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I did have the impression yesterday that you were winding up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, good morning to you. Before Mr. Zecevic resumes, I remind you you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, paragraphs 152 and 153 of your expert report and in connection with that footnote 186. One of the documents you set in that footnote is the document that is under tab 105, namely 65 ter 49D1, footnote 186.4.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please get the binders with the tabs, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I am sorry, I thought that you had them already. So we are talking about tab 105. 65 ter of the Defence, 49D1. Sir, you cited the document that you see in front of you in footnote 186 in connection with paragraph 153. Please comment.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the bylaw on the carrying out of activities in the public security service, it also foresees the monitoring of all -- monitoring, directing, and harmonising of all activities in the service. As I have pointed out in paragraph 152, this encompassed advisory supervision and the directing of organisational units -- the organisational units of the ministry outside headquarters. For example, when it comes to providing professional assistance and guidance with regard to all issues connected with the organisation of the work of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one question, please. Is this a legal obligation of the ministry headquarters with regard to its territorial units?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a legal obligation which is always further elaborated by the bylaw or rule book. In paragraph 153 I mentioned an example for this aspect of the powers of the ministry headquarters and that is the report on the -- on the inspection of the units in Dvornik [phoen] and some other places which is an example that the ministry headquarters went about such tasks in accordance with the rule book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there are objections, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do have concern. This document doesn't have a signature, doesn't have a stamp, it doesn't have a date. From the content and from other evidence in the case, I have reason to believe that it probably does relate to some work that was done in 1992, but absent this witness saying he knows the author of the document or something else to indicate that he has reason to believe that this was done in 1992, I don't think this is a witness through whom to introduce this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all due respect, in a number of documents we have seen that Mr. Tosic, Cedo was inspector in the department, the police department in -- in 1992, but I can give you the references; however, the document itself refers to the dissolution of the paramilitary and the Special Police Units. The document, the order on dissolution of these Special Police Units is exhibit in this case, just bear with me, Your Honours. If my memory serves me well, it's dated 27 July, something around there. Yes, this is Exhibit 1D176 tab 85, so I think that it's sufficient to indicate that the document is from 1992 and not to mention that we have admitted a number of documents without the stamp and the signature, I believe your own directions -- I am sorry? Guide-lines, I am sorry, yes. Your own guide-lines refer to that matter as well. So therefore I don't think this is -- this objection is founded at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, is there any chance you can find an original? I mean, we could MFI it until --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the document we received from the Office of the Prosecutor. This is their disclosure. It is not our document. I'm sorry, of course, I would be more than happy to find the original, but I must say one thing, Your Honour, it has been suggested over here over months and months the Office of the Prosecutor has been asking us for the provenance of the documents, can we have the original, where did we get it, the chain of custody and everything, only to turn at the very end that they have the document in their vaults, that it has been misplaced, it could not be found, the search engine didn't work or something like that. And I'm really -- I'm really feeling a bit frustrated, I must say, because it is imputed that the Defence is trying to, I don't know, sneak some forged documents or something which is entirely not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, there is no such perception in the Chamber. That is completely certain. We do not share any of the concerns that you have just expressed. When I was asking for an original, it was merely for the record. It's always better to have an original if we can find it than to have what appears to be a copy, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with Your Honours, but unfortunately this is what we have and what we have to live with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So in this case, the document which as you say originated from the Prosecution, this is the best that we have. Mr. Hannis, you have something to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I'm not trying to suggest that this is a forged document, I'm just saying that you as the finders of fact have this document, but we don't know when it was written, we don't know if it's a draft or if it was officially submitted or not because it's not signed, and that the information I have about where the Prosecution got this document in our MIF information sheet says this was among four binders provided by Father Marko Kljajic from Novi Sad who also wrote a book titled "How Many People Were Dying." To write this book Father Kljajic gathered documents and articles and put them together in four binders, a copy of which was handed over to investigator Stokey [phoen] on 26 June 2004. So that's where we got it and we disclosed it because it appears to be relevant. And we do know that Cedo Tosic was an investigator or inspector for the MUP and did carry out investigations. I think that's likely, but I think it's my job to try and hold us all to the standards for admissibility. Now, if it's being offered to prove that inspections were carried out by MUP inspectors in 1992, we don't contest that and we have lots of other evidence about that. We presented an inspector who testified in our case about the inspections he carried out, so if that's purpose for offering this particular one, I don't have a problem but I don't think it's necessary. We have other evidence of that. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D539, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, in paragraph 155 that deals with the same matters there is also footnote 191 that which cites document 111. That's your footnote 191.3 and the relevant document is P1341. It seems to be marked for identification. I'm not sure whether it still is. That's tab 111. Since this is a document that's cited in one of your footnotes, please make a brief comment if you can.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document too was made as a result of an audit by inspectors who were ordered to conduct that audit and to give guidance and correct monitoring. This is an annex to the report made pursuant to an order in 1992. The inspectors who carried out the audit in several SJBs made some proposals for the improving of the efficiency of the work of those SJBs. This document is cited in that footnote along with others from footnotes 186 through 191 and even 192, all these are the outcome of an organised activity launched by the ministry headquarters toward all organisational units of the MUP to enhance the work of all these units from the CSBs down to the SJBs in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this moment I really cannot remember why this document was marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't seem to have control over my microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Pick another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's the only one I have. Your Honours, as far as I can tell from reviewing the record, this was first introduced when Mr. Demirdjian was questioning a witness and he thought we were going to call an additional witness who had better relation with the document. It was MFI'd at the time. I don't have any objection to the MFI being removed, if that's what Mr. Zecevic would like to do. I'm agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So voided.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for reference, this is Exhibit P1341.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, document 119 and your footnote 192 also have to do with paragraph 155. There's a note here that this is Exhibit P407. That's under tab 113.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already pointed out and in footnote 192 I cite a document, actually a dispatch which also shows the overall activities about directing the monitoring of work, auditing, and other activities that are meant to enhance the work of the MUP. This is a dispatch that was sent from the ministry headquarters to the CSB Doboj. It says that three MUP members who carried out the audits in the territory of that centre will take over the further co-ordination of the work of one SJB and that is Bosanski Samac which is under that CSB, that they will take over the co-ordination of work, probably in order to rectify the shortcomings noted in the future period. This document is another example that the ministry headquarters really made efforts to make the organisation and functioning of all organisational units in accordance with laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bajagic, could we now please briefly discuss something as we are approaching the end of our direct examination. I'm referring to Annex 12 of your research document. Yesterday we discussed these questions partly about the relationship between the army and the police in accordance with -- in accordance with the Law on All People's Defence. I would now like to ask you to give us your comment on paragraph 8, Annex number 12, that is on the second page if you can, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 of Annex 12 which has to do with subordination of police to the army, and in relation to what we dealt with yesterday in great detail indeed, so it is Article 105 of the Law on All People's Defence of the SFRY and also it has to do with the strategy of the DSZ. I think it is page 58. I made certain comments and drew certain conclusions in this paragraph, namely that police units which are subordinated to the army act as military units. They carry out tasks from military jurisdiction, and they are in the military chain of command and responsibility, not that of the MUP or police. That is what we pointed out yesterday, bearing in mind an entire set of laws and other legislation that applied to the members of the police of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the course of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I would particularly be interested in is footnote 494 in relation to paragraph 6 and the second part of paragraph 8. Could you please give us your comment on the status?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 of this annex I say further on that members of the police lose their status as authorised officials. They are no longer in the MUP, they are no longer in civilian status because members of the MUP or the Ministry of the Interior have the status of civilians. Rather, they become combatants and therefore they can become a legitimate target of the other side in the conflict, and therefore they are subjected to military rules, not police rules. So an entire set of laws apply to them, those that deal with military issues. I base these statements of mine on what I refer to in paragraph 6, it is a convention, or rather, it is a protocol, it is the protocol to the Geneva Convention of August 1949 and in part of it, and I quoted that sentence in English even in the Serbian version of my report, and that confirms what I say in paragraph 8 and some of the other things I stated in this particular annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another matter, the second part of this annex called "co-ordination and co-ordinated action," this is what I would be interested in, I would actually like to hear your comment that sums up all of these ten paragraphs that you state here, so I am actually turning your attention to paragraph 19, the very last paragraph. Could you please give us a brief comment on paragraph 16 and 19 then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When analysing the legal framework, that is to say, all the legal regulations treating the organisation of work and functioning of the Ministry of the Interior, we saw that this is an administration organ. For that reason, and bearing in mind all the characteristics of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska as such an organ, I state that in the Ministry of the Interior there is direction as opposed to what is done in the military. In that connection at the very outset of this analysis of these terms, or rather, these concepts of co-ordination and co-ordinated action, in modern theories of management including security management and police management, generally speaking regardless of the particular activity involved, as this certainly does apply to the MUP as well, there are five functions of management or direction, if that would be the right term. There are five of them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is moving too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, I could not follow what you were saying let alone the interpreters. Just take it easy, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat those five, five ways of directing or management.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were these five functions that management or directing may have and that is planning, organisation, command, co-ordination, and control. Bearing in mind that as regards pending issues, the most important function among these five is co-ordination in terms of seeing what the relationship between the police and the military is because in 1992 in the territory of the Serb Republic of BH, I tried to state in general terms what co-ordination was. It meant co-ordinating activities of a given organisation in terms of time, place, the objective involved between two or more participants in a particular process. So if there is that kind of co-ordination, there are two or more participants. In this case of ours there are two. Further on, I said what types of co-ordination may be recognised and I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. All of that is contained in your report. However, I asked you a specific question. I asked you about 16 and 19. I asked you about co-ordinated action.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is most important is -- what is most important is in relations -- in terms of the relations between the military and the police is co-ordinated action; that is, internal co-ordination by way of subordination, as I say in paragraph 16 of this report. Ordering co-ordinated action as article -- or rather paragraph 19 says, is this kind of co-ordination by way of subordination. So in all situations it goes without saying that co-ordination by way of subordination implies co-ordinated action by way of direct orders and we see that from the legal framework involved, that implies subordination of members of the MUP to the military commander in the area where these units are being sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, whoever it is that orders co-ordinated action, does he establish this co-ordinated action at the same time for all these groups that are involved in this co-ordinated action?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Whoever it is that orders co-ordination must he in such a case or must that be the superior command for both groups whose co-ordinated action is being ordered?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The station that is issuing orders on co-ordinated action necessarily is the superior of those who are going to take part in that co-ordinated action, that is to say all of them, regardless of how many sides are involved. Whoever it is that issues the order is the superior of all of those who are taking part in this co-ordinated action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my direct examination. I just have a request. Yesterday I was reminded by the Registrar, the court deputy, that I did not tender certain documents that I had called up. That was done intentionally in some cases because I thought that the witness, or rather, that is there is not a sufficient nexus between the witness and these documents. However, there is one document pending, I hope that you will remember the document. We discussed it yesterday. Mr. Hannis was opposed to that document although I did not even tender it ultimately. He was opposed to my putting a question in that regard. Tab 12, the document is 474D1. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that the Trial Chamber did allow me to put a question, so what I would like to propose at this point in time is the following: I think that this is an important document. Could we mark it for identification? Could it be assigned a number so that in due course when we obtain the original of this document and when the Prosecutor receives it, then we can discuss it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In anticipation of your application, Mr. Zecevic, the two judges who were sitting yesterday did think through that process and that was the decision at which we arrived, so we'll have to marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D540 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Your Honours. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bajagic. We have already met but for the record my name is Dragan Krgovic. On behalf of the Defence of Stojan Zupljanin, I'm going to put questions to you related to your expert report and your testimony. I said that I would be examining you for two hours, I just have a few questions for you to clarify certain subjects that we have already discussed or rather that you already referred to during your testimony. Yesterday when answering the questions of my colleague Mr. Zecevic and Judge Delvoie, you talked about the financing of the MUP and how that problem affected the organisation and activity of the MUP in these conditions. Do you remember your testimony from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood your testimony, that part of it actually, you believe that the fact that local and regional organs financed the salaries of the MUP, gave them a certain degree of influence and they thought that they had certain rights because they were paying them, they in a way had the right to give orders to local public security stations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that particularly goes for the first period up until September 1992 when the organs of the autonomous districts and the Serb autonomous regions were still functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, could you look at number 62. P160 is the number. You cited this document, it's a brief analysis of the functioning of the MUP so far and the outlines of its future activities. Please look at page 4, or rather, it's page 5 in your binder, in E Court is 0324-1855, that's the ERN number. Number 5 in your copy and could you please look at the penultimate paragraph. It is also page 4 in the English version in e-court, I think.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appropriate page on the screen so that the other participants in these proceedings could follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As you were able to see, this is the presentation given by Stojan Zupljanin given on 11 July 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin says when he speaks about several matters including the funding of the MUP, he says the MUP and the services are funded by the government of SAO Krajina. Once the funding issue is resolved, then there will be less outside influence. Well, clearly whoever gives money wants to exert certain influence and pressurise the MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, and on the basis of this discussion I drew my conclusion with regard to the funding of the ministry. I believe I cited this document in footnote 145 and it's based on this discussion and some others that I drew my conclusions about the problems with the funding of the MUP of the Serb republic in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, please turn to page 7 in your version. That's the discussion of Mr. Andrija Bjelosevic, the chief of CSB Doboj. It's the fourth paragraph from the top. Actually, the third. I apologise. And it says, these are Bjelosevic's words: "Funding is a -- funding must be solved because whoever pays wants to issue orders and that means restraining the work of the Internal Affairs bodies."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but the English text should be on page 6. The page in Serbian is the correct page but we need another page in English, either the following page or the previous one. I apologise, it's the following page I think. It seems that this passage is not translated, at least I cannot find it. For some reason the English version of the document does not contain this passage. It probably needs to be revised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you agree with me, Mr. Bajagic, that Andrija Bjelosevic stated these words, I will read it once more: "Funding must be resolved because whoever pays wants to issue orders and that means the restraining of the work of the bodies of Internal Affairs." Is this what this passage says?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what's your comment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that not only Mr. Zupljanin's presentation --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, since we probably don't have the English, could we have an indication where on the page in B/C/S he is reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is the previous one so we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So we can locate it in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- my copy is very poor, perhaps Mr. Zecevic can assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The missing one is just after the first one. The first one, "a number of stations have no personnel and assets, it is difficult" and so on and so on, and that is exactly the one before the one which is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's clear that it is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It is entirely missing. The whole bullet is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for this, Mr. Bajagic. Can you comment this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that my views about the funding issue is based not only on the presentation of Mr. Zupljanin who was chief of CSB Banja Luka, but also on other discussions in connection with this document, including the positions put forward by the chief of CSB Doboj. At this collegium session which was held in July, we see that several CSBs point out the problem of the unresolved funding issue which probably negatively affected the work of these centres and their autonomy with regard to local political structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Bjelosevic says whoever pays want to give orders and thus restrains the bodies of the MUP and also disrupts the chain of work in the MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, because any interference with the standard operating procedures of the MUP disrupts or negatively affects the efficiency of work and certainly all other things that are required for the MUP to act in accordance with the laws and regulations as it should.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, please take a look at page 28 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ERN number is 0324-1878. And the Serbian version, that's the part where the conclusions are to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And an English page reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure about the page reference in e-court. As soon as it comes up, I'll give you this information. 024-1878 [as interpreted], conclusion number 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, when I say that the ministry was aware of the problem and that it strove to resolve it. One of the conclusions from that meeting was that more attention should be given to that problem; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conclusion 16 of the collegium of the MUP of the Serb republic held in July is very clear indeed. It says that the Ministry of the Interior must be financed exclusively from the budget of the Serb republic as stipulated by the law. At this collegium meeting, the ministry clearly shows it's commitment and its efforts to provide adequate conditions for the coming period to enable the ministry to really act as an autonomous body of public administration and tackle one of these problems or something that enables the local authorities to exert influence on the work of the organisational units of the MUP on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You will also agree with me, Mr. Bajagic, when I say that the problem was prominent throughout this initial period and that it reached into November and that there have been other discussions about this. Two corroborate that, I will show you document P1270 under your tab 68. It's the Stanisic Defence binder. You see these minutes of the extended meeting of the board of the MUP held on 5 November in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the page reference is the same in English. Possibly it could be page 4. Page 4 in English, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please take a look at the last paragraph which says: "Upon the proposal of the chief of CSB Banja Luka that a review of the MUP financing be carried out and that necessary funds be secured for salaries and equipment, in particular it was decided that for the next meeting of the board, the collegium, a relevant analysis of finances be compiled together with the Ministry of Finance." It is obvious here, Mr. Bajagic, that the problem still isn't adequately resolved. Even in November some SJBs are still faced with this same problem; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. The MUP of the Serb republic really had difficulties in its functioning in all respects, especially in the first period up until September, but even after September when they were supposed to begin functioning under new conditions, the same problems persisted partly, that is why this problem of funding is stressed and it is stated here that in co-operation with the Ministry of Finance a final solution to the problem of the funding of the ministry should be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, in your report you also dealt with the issue of communication between the ministry headquarters and the SJBs or CSBs. So let's go back to document P160. That is under tab 62 in your binder. These are the minutes of a collegium meeting, or rather the summary of a meeting of the top executives of the MUP held on 11 July. Please turn to page 5, which is page 4 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 0324-1855 is the ERN of the Serb version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the bottom of this last page, the last paragraph. These are also Zupljanin's words who says the functional communication system is destroyed. There have been talks with representatives of Rudi Cajave about acquisition of equipment. Can you tell us what Mr. Zupljanin is exactly talking about when he is saying that the communication system is destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honour. That calls for speculation on the part of this witness. He wasn't at Banja Luka. He doesn't know what was in the communication system any better than you or I do from looking at the document. Unless he can provide some further foundation, I object to this witness commenting on that entry in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't ask him what he thinks, I asked him for the meaning of this statement that the function communication system is destroyed. Not what Mr. Zupljanin meant, but what it means for the functioning of the MUP if the communication system is not functional and he as an expert should be able to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, he is an expert on police, he is not an expert on communications. He is in no better position to express an position about the meaning of that term than anyone else in this courtroom, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Except, Mr. Hannis, as I understand the question, it is as a police expert he is being asked a question about the effect in terms of police operations on this breakdown in communications, which strikes me as being permissible. Did I get the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That was my point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, can you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it says that the functional communication system has been destroyed, that means that its effect is that the possibility of communicating between the headquarters of the ministry and the organisational units, according to the territorial principle, has been completely destroyed or that it functions under far more difficult conditions. That is how I understand Mr. Zupljanin's comment on the basis of this summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And how does that effect the functioning of the MUP as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It effects the unified system of reporting and communication within the ministry and, of course, that disrupts all the lines of work and the efficiency in the discharge of all the tasks entrusted to them by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to another topic, Mr. Bajagic, one that you discussed yesterday. If you remember, you also referred to it in your expert report. It is paragraph 190 something up until 950 -- 195 onwards. You talk about the authority of authorised officials. So please look at paragraph 195 of your expert report. You refer to the Law on Internal Affairs and you speak of certain rules that were in force for awhile. Mr. Zecevic showed you one of those rule books, and I'm going to put a question to you in relation to that rule book. It is 65 ter 889D1 in Mr. Zecevic's documents. It is tab 41 in your documents. I think that it was assigned a number in the law library yesterday and I will tell you what that number is, L332. Please look at page 44. Do you have it? Sorry, I'll give you a copy. Just a moment. Could you please take a look at page 44 or 45, the ERN number is 1D05771. The B/C/S version, that is. Page 19 in the English version. So on the previous page, 43, is the use of physical force and rubber batons, as you explained in your own expert report too. So could you please look at Article 94, the last paragraph of Article 94 on page 44. Article 94, the last paragraph. This is what it says, and I'm going to quote it: "An authorised official who used a rubber truncheon or physical force has to submit within 24 hours at the latest a detailed report to his immediate superior about the reasons and intensity of the use of these means. The superior officer shall examine and assess the legality and correctness in the use of physical force and rubber truncheon and will make a note about it on the submitted report." Mr. Bajagic, that is precisely what you stated in your expert report, although that is not referred to in the law, but it is referred to in the rules. The procedure of reporting on the use of force, both in terms of rubber truncheons and fire-arms; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'm going to follow a certain sequence. I'm just going to go through all the things that should be done, how I see this line on the basis of your report. A policeman who uses force, physical force or who uses a fire-arm first submits a report to the head of his patrol if it happened while he was patrol; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then further on the commander of the department within the police station is involved in this chain, the one who is his head, that policeman's head, the policeman who used physical force; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if that is the case, if he used a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then it goes to the commander of the milicija station within the station; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then such a report is sent to the chief of the public security station; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then the chief of the public security station compiles a report along with his own assessment and then he submits it along the line of work to the CSB to the milicija department within it; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then through the chief of the public security service in the CSB, it is sent to the chief of the CSB itself; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then the chief gives his own assessment, as you say in your report, on how justified it was to use physical force; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, speaking about the minister, the chief of the CSB submits that to the head of the milicija department in the ministry headquarters; right? A report is sent to him; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably that's how such information reaches headquarters. It's not probably, that's the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then the chief of the milicija within the MUP headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It finally ends up on the desk of the undersecretary for public security, or the chief of public security in MUP, whatever he may be called; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it is only then that this is submitted to the minister if the chief believes that it is necessary to inform the minister about that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but I just notice here that if all information about anything would reach even the head of the sector of public security, let alone the minister, then they would simply be snowed under and they wouldn't have anything else to do in their lives except read all of these reports. Some things happen and then simply all of this does not go further up to higher levels. Not each and every information goes from the very bottom to the very top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You have anticipated my question. That would be the procedure to apply but in practice if this would be done in each and every case when force is applied it would be way too much, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see that this would be the right time to take the break because I'm going too move on to something else now, so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if you've been alerted, we requested to address one procedural matter before the witness resumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's why I was here but I understand Mr. Krgovic would prefer, if that's possible, he says he's got 5 minutes to complete his cross-examination, and then I'll deal very briefly with the point that I'm here for if that is' suitable to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I have to stand up also. There is one matter, Your Honours. Before the break we were discussing the insufficient translation of P160, if you remember there was the whole -- yes, the missing paragraph. Now, the situation is the following: This document has not been translated by CLSS in its entirety, this P160. This is a draft translation done by the Office of the Prosecutor, and we were instructed by the CLSS because it's a 32-page document, that CLSS does not -- are not doing the revised translations on the translations which are not their translations. Therefore, we would need the assistance of the Trial Chamber in asking the CLSS to translate this whole document, P160.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Or perhaps just to review the translation that was actually made so that they don't have to do the whole thing all over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, but I'm sure they are going to use this -- the draft translation that exists, but they are not doing the revision of the translation which is done by somebody -- by third parties, so-called. So therefore, if we can kindly ask the Trial Chamber's help in this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we make the necessary order. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, just a few more questions for you. In your expert report -- in your expert report in Annex 12, you talked about the subordination of the police, you gave your conclusion and opinion. I'll give you a few examples as to how things occurred in practice, and I'd like to hear your comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go back to document P160. It is tab 62 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It is a summary of the meeting of senior MUP personnel. It is page 4 in e-court. You have page 5. 0324-1855 is the ERN number. Just a moment, we are waiting for the English version as well. Paragraph 4 from the top of the page. Again these are Mr. Zupljanin's remarks, so it's after the parentheses he says that the role of the police should be defined and its participation in combat activity and in that connection he needs reinforcements. The army is asking for the involvement of an entire unit, they re-subordinated, and then they pushed them to the most difficult front lines which should be rendered impossible. Further on, Mr. Bajagic, the next document, please. 1D406.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, before we leave this document, could I just put a short question to the witness relating to the last sentence of paragraph 4, the sentence reads: "The active duty units had to be reinforced through educating courses on the MUP level, or within the area of Banja Luka." Mr. Bajagic, are you able to cast some light over the background of this remark by Mr. Zupljanin? What lies behind here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, it's not that they are only admitted but during their career, members of the MUP, especially the active-duty personnel continue to have an obligation to be trained further and to become well versed in new skills so that they could carry out the tasks as defined by law. Mr. Zupljanin is probably trying to say here that personnel should be trained further at the level of the ministry as a whole and then he also says within the Banja Luka region. These courses can be general courses or specialised courses as envisaged by the system of police training and education and they can also be organised at the level of one security centre, not only at the level of the entire ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that, but my question is really whether there had been any incidents that would specifically call for the need to train the active police, and this again begs the next question, what about the reserve police, how were they trained? But my interest is really why was there suddenly a need to have extra education or training of the police force? Was there any -- had there been any incidents that would call for this or was Mr. Zupljanin's remark here just an expression of the ordinary general necessity of keeping your police force well trained at all times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is certainly an expression of this general need, no matter what conditions the ministry members work under in order to discharge their duties they must permanently train.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, I apologise, part of what I've read out is missing in the translation, so I would like to comment on this paragraph with you. Please return to that section of the text. Mr. Zupljanin speaks about two things here, one is the participation of the police in combat activities, that is, re-subordination, and then he also speaks about manning. These are the two subjects he speaks about in this item, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in the first part of this sentence he speaks about re-subordination and how the army behaves on the ground. They take the entire police unit, resubordinate it, and it pushes them to the most difficult sections of the front line, as well as that this should be curtailed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then he speaks about the manning of the police force and the need that regular manning should take place through courses at MUP level and training the reserve force; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in connection with these remarks made by Mr. Zupljanin, please take a look at 1D406, tab 23 in your binder. This is an order by General Talic from July 1992. It precedes these remarks by Mr. Zupljanin we saw -- we have just seen. We commented on the -- on a paragraph on the following page with Mr. Zecevic. It's the third paragraph from the bottom. It says: "In the carrying out of combat activities all police forces are placed under the command of the zone commander who decides about their use." This is what Mr. Zupljanin was referring to, that the entire police force from a municipality is placed under the control of a military commander and thus the activities of the MUP in a certain territory are totally paralyzed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I clarify additionally. This is one of the problems I noted while I was writing my expert report. Many police officers from a territory, if not all, are re-subordinated to an army commander which makes the discharge of their regular duties very difficult or impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And such a practice prevailed until September, namely that without consulting the chief of the CSB or the minister, the police was re-subordinated in this manner and used for these purposes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That is not in line with the procedure you were explaining in annex 12, namely how this re-subordination process should be gone about, only under certain conditions and so on; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was explaining that the organisational levels in the territory where the re-subordination of some police members takes place should know about it, maybe the CSB or another organisational unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, could I just hold you on to the document which is still on the screen, the order by General Talic, because the part that was read out by Mr. Krgovic says that "in the conduct of combat activities all police forces shall be placed under the command of the army commander," but what does the term "conduct of combat activities" actually mean? Because I suppose that in the normal practice of events, there would be, say, an armed operation, a military operation that would involve, say, an attack on a legitimate target, so there will be shelling and subsequently there would be the moving in of armed forces into the area. But what would happen once the mission was accomplished? You would still have the police forces present in the area but the armed activity had come to an end. Would the police forces there then still be under the command of the army commander, or would we assume that the armed activities had come to an end and so as of that moment the command over the police forces would then go back to the CSB or to the SJB, to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? The military commander to who a unit is subordinated and that unit is made up of MUP members decides about the period during which the MUP members are subordinated. Combat activities need not mean offensive operations, they could also be defensive operations, but these are military matters, I don't want to go into that. While they were subordinated they don't have the status of authorised officials. They will get it back only once they are back in the organisational unit, be it the CSB or the SJB, that is when the status of being subordinated ceases, they go back to their regular duties and are again entitled to their regular powers as stipulated by the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but just on the border-line between being under the army command and returning to their MUP command, that particular point in time, how is that decided? Was that just by the fact that they returned back to their police station or was it required that the army commander officially release them back to the MUP? Do you understand my question? I'm looking -- because I'm looking for the constitutive elements that transfers the authority over police forces from the army back to the MUP because my impression is that there is really a grey zone there, once the combat activities have come to an end then there is a grey zone until they are clearly and definitely back into their MUP positions, their original MUP positions. So I would be glad if you could help us shed some light over the mechanisms that would transfer the authority back from the army to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military commander to who in a certain zone of responsibility everybody is subordinated at the end of military preparations assesses that these operations are finished and informs the officer of that other organisation that these MUP members can return to the regular duties in the MUP. Then these MUP members are transported by some means of transportation from that military zone of responsibility to their respective organisational units of the MUP. Then by arriving at their organisational unit, they again receive the status of authorised officials. Certainly the unit returning from such a task will get a few days of leave, but basically as soon as they return to their organisational unit they are again members of the ministry. I hope I was able to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You were certainly, but let me just clarify that the constitutive element here would be an order issued by the military commander to release the police forces back to their regular duties, is that correctly understood, that there would have to be an order by the army commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not analyse the procedure applied by military commanders, but it's natural to me that the military commander to whom everybody is subordinated must be the one to say to all participants that their task is completed and that they can return to their regular duties. That seems natural to me. What kind of document is involved or maybe it's just an oral order, I cannot say, but certainly the commander to who everybody is subordinated in his zone of responsibility decides that their mission is completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I take you back to the document that was shown to you by Mr. Krgovic, namely the rule book on the operational methods. I think the document is 65 ter number 889 or it's in the law library L332. And I would like us to have a look at Article 94 once again. While we are waiting for the document to pop up on the screen, Mr. Bajagic, my question to you as an academic and as a professor, I'm sure that you would no doubt have come across the fact that very often what is written in the rules diverge significantly from what is the actual reality, and so my question to you when you describe in your report in the paragraphs 190 to 195, when you describe the rules about the reporting, that is a very clear and exhaustive description of the procedures that would apply to the reporting, but my question to you is, do you have any sense of how this was applied in practice? Because I'm sure that during a war time things did not always function the way they should according to the rules, so how effective was really the reporting in 1992, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my report I devoted some attention, especially in the paragraphs you mentioned, to the authority to use force, including firearms, since these are very sensitive issues regarding the actions of members of the MUP in general, this applies to every police force. I did mention in my report that apart from what I called the set of means of force, the use of fire-arms certainly is a most sensitive issue and in any police force, including the MUP of the RS is considered the ultimate means to carry out a task efficiently. I devoted special attention to some articles of the Law on Internal Affairs and other pieces of legislation that regulate this subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Professor, please be brief and try to answer my question, how was all of this -- how did this come out in practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly all the procedures as laid down by the law and bylaws are not always honoured in practice. I cannot make an estimate now about the number of instances when they were not honoured, or I cannot give you a percentage, because I haven't critically reviewed the situation in reality, but I'm sure that as in any police force, there must have been omissions and shortcomings in this respect, but I didn't have information to give any -- to state any particulars in these paragraphs in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you wanted to raise a matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, Your Honour. Your Honours, I don't think it matters much but maybe -- I don't know if he speaks English, maybe the professor should remove his earphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Bajagic could you remove your headphones for the time being, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, he does speak English. Oh well. I thought that was right. Well, Your Honours, it doesn't matter because he can certainly stay here rather than having to leave court. Your Honours, I am here and I apologise for interrupting this witness, but as I said to Your Honours it's perhaps an urgent matter that needs to be resolved. You will recall on Monday, the Defence, Mr. O'Sullivan requested that the Prosecution be precluded from using certain documents in cross-examination of the witness who is to return. I said that it would help if we were provided with a list of those documents for which they say we should not be allowed to use in cross, and they did so helpfully and I think it was copied to the Legal Officer, and I hope Your Honours have got a copy because it's easier if I refer to that. Your Honours, can I say this is clearly linked with the request by the Defence that we should -- that the Trial Chamber should order us to provide all the material which they refer to in their motion which includes the correspondence over disclosure under 66(B). Your Honours, can I just briefly put this into context. As Your Honours saw, there was the request in October of 2009 which was an all encompassing request which we declined to comply with and we included our response. After that we had specific requests under Rule 66(B) which are not copied, but Your Honours one of them, as I remarked earlier, was on the 21st of January of this year which requested all documents signed by Mr. Bjelosevic. And we extended that to documents that are actually being provided by him. Your Honours, in the list that was provided, Your Honours, the only documents which fall under that specific request of the 21st of January are those at 5, 6, 16, 30, 34, and 90. The rest are all documents that we propose to use in cross-examination of the returning witness, but they do not fall under that specific request or any other request save for the very late one which, as we say, is far too broad and is merely an attempt to get in advance the documentation we are going to use for cross-examination, particularly going to credibility of witnesses and which under the -- Your Honours' guide-lines we do not have to disclose until the witness has started his evidence. And there's good reason for that. Your Honours, all 5, 6, 16, 30, and 34 and 90 were all documents provided by Mr. Bjelosevic when he was interviewed in 2004 and 2009, and I referred to them when I dealt with the whole matter. We accept that we should -- when we disclosed the interviews in 2009, and I emphasise that so the Defence had the interviews since July 2009, we should have also sent the documents with it. We didn't, but the Defence told you that they were using our interviews as the basis for calling Mr. Bjelosevic. At no stage did we ever have a request for these documents, which would have reminded us, if nothing else, that we hadn't disclosed them. The documents provided are discussed during the course of the interview, some in more details than others. If we take one example, which is the document number 5, that's discussed at page 83 of the 2004 interview. I number them consecutively but it's discussed. Number 6 is discussed at page 22 and so on and so forth. Your Honours, we say the Defence have suffered no prejudice at all and that there is -- they've shown no good reason other than attempt to punish the Prosecution which is not the goal, we submit, of any rulings that Your Honours should make. Your Honours should look at is there any prejudice which has been shown to the Defence by us not disclosing those six documents under the specific request and we say there isn't. And as regards the others, we say they do not come under any proper request under Rule 66(B) and that's the submissions we make. Your Honours, as I say, I know that Mr. Hannis has reminded you about the need for a decision on Mr. Nielsen, but obviously I do think this is a fairly important matter as well that Your Honours should deal with perhaps before the return the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we've already indicated we are very much aware of the fact that it has to be dealt with before Mr. Bjelosevic returns. But it is something that requires -- I was going to say, thank you, Judge, a closer look, because we wish to carefully state what we have to say on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that. Then Your Honours, I see Mr. O'Sullivan is going to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, may I briefly respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I think now, if anything, we see that there have been in fact two breaches by the Prosecution in relation to Bjelosevic. First there was non-disclosure with the statement in 2009, and second, as is conceded, there is a breach of Rule 66(B) as recently as January of this year. Now, as for prejudice, it's not a matter of seeking relief to punish the Prosecution, the relief we seek is to ensure a fair trial. Rule 66(B) disclosure is intended to be material which is used by the Defence in preparation of its defence. Had the Prosecution complied with its obligation under 66(B), we would have been in a position to have had these documents prior to the commencement of Mr. Bjelosevic's testimony, it would have been used in the preparation of our Defence case and our preparation of his testimony. And that's the prejudice to us. The only relief at this point which is commensurate with that breach is to not allow the Prosecution to use those documents during its cross-examination. So the basis for the relief is the guarantee of the fair trial and proper preparation. That's why we seek the relief requested.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am sorry, I didn't quite understand the reference to non-disclosure of the statement by Mr. Bjelosevic. We disclosed the 2004 and 2009 interviews in 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, but I understood the Prosecutor to say that there was not full disclosure along with those statements. In any case, the true violation is a 66(B) request which was made in January of this year for which there is acknowledged a violation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could I hear you on one small point, Mr. O'Sullivan, your submission that the relief at this point which commensurate with that breach is to not allow the Prosecution to use those documents during its cross-examination, what about the -- what to my mind seems an obvious alternative, but you may have a contrary view, is to allow the Defence to deal with these documents before the cross-examination begins?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, are you suggesting with your leave we would be able to meet with the witness for the limited purposes of dealing with these documents, am I understanding you correctly, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know whether the question of meeting with the witness arises, but having been provided with these documents if there are matters which should have been explored, which your appreciation then is they should have been explored in cross-examination, I would have thought that it is certainly -- and leave could be sought to re-open the examination-in-chief on the one hand and cross-examination of the second accused on the other hand before the cross-examination by the Prosecution begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, our position is that the proper application of the Rule 66(B) is that we are entitled to this information prior to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm not losing sight of that. It's just that I wanted to hear you on what struck me as being an obvious response. What I am saying may not be the position taken by the Prosecution, it's just that for myself and Judge Harhoff agrees, and probably Judge Delvoie as well, that that is an alternative; in other words, the sanction that you purport is not the only option, that's the only question I'm asking. If you have a view on that, fine. If not, it's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may intervene, Your Honours. Your Honours, I explained very clearly the first time I raised this matter and objected. The problem is at hand is Mr. Bjelosevic, but what we are trying to establish is that there is violations of disclosure. There are disclosure violations. And now Mr. Bjelosevic is our first witness, now with this witness we have the same thing repeating again. And that is going to happen until the end of the Defence case with each and every witness that is coming because a number of documents have been withheld from us. We say the Office of the Prosecutor should not be allowed to do that. We made the request in 2009, 66(B), the Office of the Prosecutor said well, it's too broad, but we assure you that we are giving you everything. We said, okay. Then we gave specific requests, but still understanding that the words written by the Office of the Prosecutor means that they are actually disclosing to us all the relevant material. Now we come to the point where Ms. Korner says, well, it wasn't specific whether he signed whether he was given, maybe it is the document that he received from somebody, I mean, if we are going into such details, then, then our request from 2009 is specific enough because we said everything. Give us everything. So now -- but you see, Your Honours, if I want to -- if I want to specify each and every possibility, it would take me 4.000 pages to say every possible -- whether this was connected with Mr. Mico Stanisic during the time when he was in his, I don't know, school or it was connected with the people who were in relation to him in his office or something like that. The problem, Your Honour, is that we rely on the rules and the obligation of the Office of the Prosecutor and on their professionalism that they disclose to us the documents that they are bound to disclose to us by the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but this is not how I understand the issue. If we are talking of these six documents here, there's no discussion about the fact that they should have been disclosed. The Prosecutor admits that. So your argumentation is not relevant with respect to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: To other documents, and you are referring probably to what seems to be 28 documents on the cross-examination list for this witness also, there I think the question is were they under an obligation -- was the Prosecutor under an obligation to disclose or not, and if not, if there was no obligation under 66(B) or 68 as such, can they put them on their list for cross-examination only for the purpose of cross-examination. And is your position that they can't for documents where there is no disclosure obligation as such under 66(B) or 68?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, of course not, Your Honours. I think some of the documents. We discussed with Mr. Hannis about this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe the usher can escort the witness for just a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We discussed with Mr. Hannis about the number of documents that have been shown to us for the first time. Now, Mr. Hannis assured us that this is just for the limited purposes of testing the credibility of the witness, not for the truth of its contents, but to test the credibility of the witness, and we said okay. We said okay. I mean, of course we don't think that this is a violation of 66(B). Now, but today we received a number of documents which have nothing to do with the testing of credibility of the witness but are in fact the documents concerning the finances of the MUP which have never ever been disclosed to us, which is a violation of 66(B) or 68, and I still didn't have time to review them. But what I'm trying to say, Your Honours, is that this situation we will have repeating over and over and losing the precious court time because the problem is here. And the Office of the Prosecutor acknowledges the problem but still maintains the position that they should be allowed to do that, and we say they shouldn't because there must be somewhere must be -- the line must be drawn and the understanding must be clear what can be done and what cannot be done. That is my sincere opinion, because with this situation we have made a specific request a week ago after this first situation with Bjelosevic, specific request for each and every witness. We got the response from the Office of the Prosecutor that it's too broad. Now, we had to file the motion to compel the Prosecution to -- so what I'm trying to say, it's building up and the problem is not solved. And the problem is actually really hurting the Defence because we have this witness on the stand, Mr. Bjelosevic is coming, then is the next witness after him, then Mr. Bjelosevic cross, then another witness, so the problem will only enlarge and we will be prejudiced because of that. Thank you. Sorry I took sometime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, can I respond because effectively Mr. Zecevic has expanded out of the specific problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, just to follow up what I asked Mr. Zecevic and his answer was no, we don't -- we don't oppose documents that are only there on your list for the purposes of cross-examination and that were under no prior disclosure obligation. Okay. So I take that as his position. Now, is it your position that you can put on your -- on that list for cross-examination documents that you did not disclose but that should have been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we put on our list documents that we should have disclosed either under a specific proper, I underline that, Rule 66(B) request, and/or 68, which are the two methods of disclosure, then Your Honours have to look at the principle of whether the Defence have suffered prejudice or how the failure to disclose came about, as opposed to an automatic rejection. So, Your Honours, can I return for a moment to the six documents on this list. In fact, the Defence had disclosure in terms of notification and description of the documents through the interviews. They didn't have the actual documents but they had notification, as I say, and disclosure and I am sorry, Your Honours, but there is a certain responsibility on the Defence if they consider that these documents contained in the interviews of the witnesses which they assured the Court were the basis of calling this witness, then they bear a certain amount of responsibility, in civil law terms, if damages were being assessed they would be contributory, I don't know if you have the same, but in England it's called contributory liability. Your Honours, but I want to return to the general principle that Mr. Zecevic says is on-going problem. The original request in October which is attached to their motion, Your Honour, one only has to read it out to see that this cannot be a proper request. "Inspection of all books, documents, photographs, tangible objects intended to be used at trial. Inspections of all books, documents, photographs, tangible objects belonging to Zupljanin or Stanisic. Inspection of all books, documents, photographs, and tangible objects which are material to the preparation of the Defence. This would include all information received from persons who have personal knowledge of the events in the indictment but whom the Prosecution does not intend to call as witnesses in chief." That would mean every statement ever taken for the purposes of any trial that relates to any events in the indictment, and for Prijedor alone I imagine that was thousands of statements. "All information from persons who have testified as Defence witnesses in cases dealing with any of the same events to be proved in this case. All -- all this --" and I'm quoting, "all information received from the Bosnian government or any of its entities including its courts pertaining to the accused or the events to be proved in this case." Your Honours have got the document, I'm not going to go on, but you can see it is a wholly ludicrous fishing expedition which were it to be complied with would mean the trial would never have got started at all, the Defence would spend years looking at all of this, and that is why we say this -- why we wrote back saying this is not a proper application. And Your Honours, as I say, since then, the Defence never wrote back again saying yes it is, and unless you comply we will be putting it before the Court, instead of which sensibly they sent us proper requests relating to specific subjects, such as, for example, all interviews we had conducted with members of the MUP over the years. Your Honours, the Defence are actually -- their problem is this: That they are calling witnesses who like many of the witnesses we called, but there we had an obligation to disclose the information we had, were a party to these events. As Mr. Zecevic said on one occasion, it is our contention that Mr. Bjelosevic is a party to the joint criminal enterprise which we say existed at the time. And therefore what they are trying to do by their latest request is, as I say, get around the fact that we are not obliged to disclose until such time as Mr. Bjelosevic goes into the witness box, the information that we have which relates to his credibility as a witness. And that is what they are trying to do by the latest attempt at what they call a 66(B) attempt which is no better than this particular one there. And that is why we object and that is the ruling that Your Honours have got to make. To what extent under the guise, if I put it that way, of Rule 66(B) are the Prosecution -- sorry, are the Defence entitled to know in advance what documents we have which relate to the credibility of their witness. And that's the simple issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so as I said, we are giving this careful consideration and I trust that we would put this matter to rest although that may be an expression of judicial naivete but we will see. Sorry, Mr. Zecevic. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm grateful for Ms. Korner's enlightenment about our intentions. I wasn't even aware of it myself. The point of the matter, Your Honours, is the following: It's the obligation of the Office of the Prosecution to comply with the Rule 68 and 66(B). It has nothing to do with any of our intensions protecting any of the witnesses or whatever. It is very strict point, that the obligation according to the rules rests with the Prosecution to disclose Rule 68 material to the Defence. And on request of Defence to disclose 66(B) and that's what we ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think the witness can be escorted back in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honours excludes me then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, you may go, Ms. Korner. We have a brief ruling [Microphone not activated]. Thanks. The Chamber is seized of a motion filed on the 21st of April whereby the Stanisic Defence requests reconsideration of or in the alternative certification to appeal an oral decision of 19th of April. By this decision, the Chamber denied admission into evidence of certain documents which the Defence considered relevant under Rule 68 to challenge Christian Nielsen's credibility as an expert. The Chamber found that these documents do not challenge the credibility of the expert or that of his reports admitted in this case. The Chamber recalling that it issued the decision in the exercise of its discretion, holds the Defence has not demonstrated a clear error of reasoning in the 19th of April decision. Moreover, it finds that it is not necessary to reconsider the decision to prevent an injustice. In respect of the request for certification, the Defence refers to the Prosecution's announcement that it will use Christian Nielsen's report during the cross-examination of the Defence expert currently on the stand. It submits that an important issue in dispute between the parties is the bias or objectivity of Christian Nielsen as a former staff member of the Prosecution.
